one_line: Better Stack demo of the anti-slop rule package for oxlint, which hard-fails low-evidence TypeScript/JavaScript patterns and whose error messages give coding agents a fix to apply.
summary: The speaker argues that CLAUDE.md rules are easy for agents to ignore, while lint rules are a deterministic hard fail that is also cheaper in tokens. The tool is the anti-slop rule package for oxlint, a Rust-based JS/TS linter from Oxc. The point is to hand-pick the rules that match your team's standards, not to enable all of them. A demo file with double type assertions (unknown, then a User type) and a function returning unknown shows descriptive errors that name the problem and the fix, such as validating at the boundary with Zod or returning a named domain type. Claude Code is asked to "fix all issues in api client"; it runs the lint script after each edit and repairs until clean, taking a few minutes. The speaker says lint errors are not bugs in themselves but catch the lost type evidence that later causes bugs, such as an API date that is really a string. The package was created the week before, and the speaker claims oxlint is 50 to 100 times faster than ESLint without showing a benchmark. The video is short, has no sponsor segment, and ends with a subscribe request.

key_ideas.idea: Lint rules beat CLAUDE.md rules for keeping slop out: agents can ignore or work around prose rules, while a lint failure is deterministic and cheaper in tokens.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says no amount of CLAUDE.md tweaking reliably stops slop, and that linting is a hard fail on the patterns you want out.

key_ideas.idea: anti-slop is a set of oxlint rules that reject low-evidence TypeScript and JavaScript patterns, and you should hand-pick the subset that matches your team's standards.
key_ideas.detail: The package has many rules, including chain type assertions, unknown parameters and unknown returns. The speaker says the point is not to enable all of them.

key_ideas.idea: Lint error messages explain why and how to fix, which makes them useful feedback for an agent in a way raw TypeScript errors are not.
key_ideas.detail: Example messages: an assertion chain discards type evidence (fix: keep the original precise type or validate untrusted input at the boundary, e.g. with Zod); a function exposes unknown to its caller (fix: validate at the boundary and return a named domain type).

key_ideas.idea: Run the agent in a generate, lint, repair loop: the lint script in package.json runs oxlint on the source, and Claude fixes its own errors.
key_ideas.detail: The demo prompt was 'fix all issues in api client'. Claude ran for a few minutes and cleared all flagged issues, with almost all rules enabled in the lint config.

key_ideas.idea: Lint findings are not bugs, but they catch the lost type evidence that becomes bugs.
key_ideas.detail: Casting an API response to an Account type where created is a Date compiles, yet JSON returns a string. Because the cast discarded the evidence, TypeScript cannot warn, and the first date operation fails.

key_ideas.idea: The package is new and built on oxlint, which the speaker presents as much faster than ESLint.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says the package was created last week, that he has used it for months, and that some users reported more slop errors than they expected.

techniques.name: Hand-picked lint gate for agent-written TS/JS
techniques.how: Install the anti-slop rules for oxlint, add a lint script to package.json that runs oxlint on the source directory, enable only the rules that match team standards (the speaker's demo config enables almost all), and make lint a required pass before an agent's change is accepted.
techniques.when: A TypeScript or JavaScript repo where agents write code and CLAUDE.md rules are being ignored.

techniques.name: Agent self-repair loop on lint output
techniques.how: Prompt the agent to fix all issues in a module (the demo used 'fix all issues in api client'). The agent writes code, runs the lint script, reads the rule messages, and repairs until the linter exits clean.
techniques.when: Cleaning up or generating a module where the lint messages state the fix precisely enough for the agent to act without extra prompting.

techniques.name: Validate untrusted input at the boundary instead of casting
techniques.how: Replace chained casts such as as unknown as User on JSON responses with a runtime schema (the speaker names Zod) at the API boundary. Return a named domain type from the function rather than unknown.
techniques.when: Any code that receives JSON from an API and would otherwise use type assertions to make the compiler accept it.

tools: oxlint (Oxc; Rust-based JavaScript and TypeScript linter)
anti-slop (rule package for oxlint; created the week before the video)
Oxc (the toolchain that oxlint belongs to)

numbers.claim: Speaker says oxlint is benchmarked at 50 to 100 times faster than ESLint. The speaker shows no benchmark, so treat it as an unverified claim.
Claude completed the 'fix all issues in api client' task in a few minutes (roughly 2-3 minutes).

The anti-slop package was created about one week before the video. The speaker has used it on his projects for a few months, which is inconsistent with the package's age and is probably a slip in the transcript.

hot_takes: Lint rules are a deterministic gate on agent output and beat CLAUDE.md prose rules, which agents ignore.
Linters are not new, but their explanatory messages are now useful input for coding agents.
Do not enable every rule in an anti-slop-style package; choose the subset your team agrees on.
Unverified: oxlint is 50 to 100 times faster than ESLint (no benchmark shown).

relevance.why: The video targets TypeScript and JavaScript code quality. AgentOS is described as Rust and Python infrastructure, so the rules do not apply.
ProsHarness runs Claude Code in loops and checkpoints. A deterministic lint step after each agent edit, with rule messages fed back, fits that loop better than CLAUDE.md rules.
relevance.action: Add a lint step to the ProsHarness edit-and-repair loop for TS or JS targets, with the rule messages passed back to the agent, and measure how many fix iterations it saves.
